ABSTRACT


Abstract

Introduction:

Having

children

is

the

life

project

of

many

couples,

but

this

dream

can

be

affected

by

infertility,

which

affects

about

15%

of

people

worldwide.

Given

this

high

prevalence,

assisted

reproduction

treatments

have

gained

notoriety

and

have

become

an

alternative

for

many

individuals.

Furthermore,

advances

in

medicine

have

significantly

increased

oocyte

donation,

which

can

have

a

profound

emotional

impact

on

both

egg

donors

and

recipients,

potentially

decreasing

the

quality

of

life

(QoL)

of

these

women.

Objective:

This

study

aims

to

assess

the

quality

of

life

of

female

egg

donors

and

recipients,

as

well

as

infertile

women

who

will

undergo

assisted

reproduction

treatment

but

will

not

be

donors

or

recipients.

Method:

Prospective

cross-sectional

study

in

which

the

FERTIQOL

questionnaire

was

used

to

assess

QoL

and

a

sociodemographic

questionnaire

was

administered

to

60

women

undergoing

treatment

at

an

assisted

reproduction

clinic

in

Porto

Alegre,

Rio

Grande

do

Sul.

Result:

According

to

the

collected

data,

a

significant

difference

was

observed

in

the

total

FERTIQOL

score

(p<0.001).

In

the

domains

covered

by

the

instrument,

the

results

were

also

significant,

with

mind

and

body

p<0.001,

emotional

p<0.001,

relational

p=0.040,

and

social

p=0.018.

The

26

women

undergoing

treatment

without

donating

or

receiving

eggs

had

lower

quality-of-life

scores,

as

measured

by

FERTIQOL

total

and

all

domains,

compared

to

the

15

recipients

and

19

donors.

Conclusion:

Women

undergoing

assisted

reproductive

treatment

experience

emotional

distress

during

the

treatment,

resulting

in

a

reduced

quality

of

life

when

compared

with

women

who

undergo

the

oocyte

donation

process

during

treatment.

um

estigma,

visto

que

ainda

ocorre

uma

pressão

social

associada

à

procriação,

acarretando

culpa

pela

não

efetivação

da

gestação.

Outrossim,

de

acordo

com

Wdowiak

et

al

(2021),

as

críticas

relacionadas

ao

não

engravidar

são

direcionadas

às

mulheres.

De

acordo

com

esse

mesmo

autor,

estudos

demonstram

que

a

infertilidade

pode

reduzir

a

qualidade

de

vida

de

casais

inférteis.




2.2

INFERTILIDADE

A

infertilidade

pode

ser

definida

como

a

dificuldade

de

obter

e/ou

manter

a

gestação.

Aliás,

existem

duas

diferentes

categorizações

de

infertilidade,

classificadas

como

primária

e

secundária.

A

infertilidade

primária

é

caracterizada

por

um

casal

que

não

conseguiu

conceber

desde

a

primeira

tentativa.

Já

a

secundária

é

quando

o

casal

já

teve

uma

gestação,

independentemente

do

desfecho,

e

não

consegue

engravidar

novamente

(Hayashi

e

Moriyama,

2019).

Em

1978,

com

o

nascimento

do

primeiro

bebê

por

fertilização

in

vitro,

novas

perspectivas

se

abrem

para

esses

casais

que,

muitas

vezes,

se

viam

sem

esperança.

A

infertilidade

é

um

tema

tabu,

fazendo

com

que

os

casais

tenham

grande

dificuldade

de

expor

o

que

estão

vivenciando

(Awtani

et

al,

2019).


Além

disso,

a

questão

da

infertilidade

pode

gerar

diversos

sentimentos

em

quem

recebe

o

diagnóstico,

como

culpa

e

vergonha.

Esse

diagnóstico

pode

acarretar

o

isolamento

social,

bem

como

sentimentos

de

inferioridade,

desencadeando

quadros

de

ansiedade

e

depressão

(Marciano

et

al

2024).


Ainda

em

função

do

tratamento

de

fertilização

in

vitro,

as

mulheres

podem

vir

a

apresentar,

além

das

emoções

já

citadas,

como

ansiedade

e

estresse,

problemas

relacionados

à

autoestima,

dificuldade

de

relacionamento

com

o

parceiro

e

com

os

demais,

podendo

ocasionar

isolamento

social

(Wojciechowska;

Milska-Musa,

2024).


Alguns

estudos

evidenciam

diferenças

no

enfrentamento

da

infertilidade

e

no

tratamento

entre

homens

e

mulheres.

De

acordo

com

Yi-Ling

Hsu

et

al.

(2002),

as

esposas

despendem

mais

energia

e

tempo

com

os

tratamentos

de

reprodução

assistida,

e

por

isso

se

sentem

mais

exigidas

durante

o

tratamento

(Awtani

et

al.,

2019).

Também

apresentam

maior

índice

de

ansiedade

e

depressão

em

comparação

com

seus

parceiros.


Durante

o

período

de

tratamento,

os

casais

precisam

tomar

uma

série

de

decisões

difíceis,

reiterando

que

possivelmente

a

decisão

mais

difícil

se

dá

no

momento

da

falha

do

tratamento,

quando

o

casal

precisa

se

reorganizar

financeiramente

e

emocionalmente

(Chan

et

al

2016).


Os

problemas

de

fertilização

trazem

prejuízos

físicos

e

emocionais

aos

casais,

envolvendo

períodos

de

exames

para

a

investigação

de

infertilidade

e

o

próprio

tratamento.

Esse

período

é

marcado

por

inseguranças

e

uma

série

de

incertezas

(Song

et

al,

2021).


De

acordo

com

Jing

(2021),

há

diferentes

tratamentos

de

reprodução

assistida

que

podem

ser

utilizados,

dependendo

da

causa

da

infertilidade.

Um

dos

tratamentos

utilizados

é

a

fertilização

in

vitro

(FIV).


A

FIV

apresenta

um

desenvolvimento

tecnológico

significativo

desde

o

primeiro

bebê

em

1978.

Com

tais

mudanças,

os

tratamentos

de

reprodução

assistida

foram

sendo

cada

vez

mais

estudados

e

pesquisados,

ganhando

notoriedade

em

razão

de

seus

resultados.

A

fertilização

in

vitro

possibilita

hoje

que

a

gestação

ocorra

em

mulheres

de

maneira

solo,

em

casais

homoafetivos

e

em

casais

inférteis,

inclusive

a

partir

da

doação

de

esperma

ou

óvulos.

O

ciclo

da

FIV,

que

geralmente

dura

aproximadamente

15

(quinze)

dias,

tem

início

com

a

estimulação

ovariana,

passa

pela

aspiração

dos

folículos

e

termina

com

a

transferência

do

embrião

(Eskew

&

Jungheim,

2017).



2.3

OVODOAÇÃO


Uma

das

formas

de

realização

da

FIV

envolve

óvulos

doados.

O

compar
tilhamento

anônimo

de

óvulos

é

geralmente

realizado

por

mulheres

em

tratamento

com

FIV,

que,

assim,

poderão

doar

parte

de

seus

óvulos.

Cada

país

tem

sua

norma

para

a

doação

(
Asplund,

2020).



No

Brasil,

o

Conselho

Federal

de

Medicina

(CFM)

é

o

órgão

responsável

por

regulamentar

as

técnicas

de

reprodução

assistida.

De

acordo

com

a

Resolução

CFM

nº

2.320/2022,

a

doação

de

gametas

é

permitida

sem

que

haja

fins

lucrativos

ou

comercialização

e

deve

ser

realizada

de

forma

sigilosa

tanto

para

a

doadora

quanto

para

a

receptora.

O

único

momento

em

que

o

anonimato

não

ocorre

é

na

doação

familiar,

quando

a

receptora

poderá

receber

oócitos

de

familiar

com

parentesco

de

até

4º

grau.

A

ovodoação

poderá

ser

realizada

por

mulheres

de

até

37

(trinta

e

sete)

anos.

Ainda,

de

acordo

com

o

CFM,

a

doação

de

gametas

pode

ser

realizada

voluntariamente

ou

por

meio

de

doação

compartilhada.

Na

segunda

opção,

doadora

e

receptora

compartilharão

do

material

biológico

e

dos

custos

envolvidos

(CONSELHO

FEDERAL

DE

MEDICINA,

2022).


Os

aspectos

legais

relativos

à

doação

de

gametas

variam

de

país

para

país.

No

Reino

Unido,

por

exemplo,

é

permitido

o

contato

com

a

doadora

após

atingir

a

maioridade,

o

que

oferece

a

oportunidade

de

reconhecer

sua

história

genética.

Essa

possibilidade

suscita

preocupação

com

o

vínculo

e

medo

de

rejeição

por

parte

da

receptora.

Diante

desse

contexto,

nos

países

em

que

a

doação

é

anônima,

a

maioria

relata

sentir

maior

tranquilidade

(Bracewell-Milnes,

2016).


Um

estudo

realizado

em

Taiwan,

país

muito

reconhecido

pelos

tratamentos

de

reprodução

assistida

do

continente

asiático,

aborda

o

incentivo

às

mulheres

doadoras

de

óvulos,

o

que

promove

o

altruísmo.

Apesar

de

não

poder

ser

comercializado,

o

incentivo

financeiro

é

altamente

atrativo,

levando

as

doadoras

a

receber

cerca

de

3

mil

dólares

por

ciclo.

Mesmo

com

tal

incentivo,

as

doadoras

relatam

que

a

principal

motivação

é

o

desejo

de

ajudar

outras

mulheres

(Chen,

2025).


No

que

se

refere

à

escolha

entre

uma

doadora

anônima

ou

uma

conhecida,

alguns

estudos

apontam

que

a

doação

anônima

oferece

maior

segurança,

permitindo

que

as

mulheres

estabeleçam

limites

mais

definidos

entre

as

partes

envolvidas

(Bracewell-Milnes,

2016).


Referente

à

doação

de

oócitos,

diante

do

viés

psicológico,

há

diferentes

motivações,

como

o

altruísmo,

a

contribuição

científica

e

questões

financeiras.

De

acordo

com

um

estudo

sueco,

o

altruísmo

predomina

nessa

tomada

de

decisão,

mas,

assim,

traz

um

sentimento

ambivalente

à

doadora

(Svanberg,

Lampic

&

Gejervall,

2012).



Outra

questão

que

faz

com

que

as

doadoras

de

óvulos

hesitem

em

sua

decisão

é

a

própria

natureza

do

tratamento,

que

demanda

procedimentos

invasivos,

além

do

uso

de

hormônios,

o

que

traz

sobrecarga

e

desgaste,

tanto

físicos

quanto

emocionais

(Bracewell-Milnes,

2016).

Outro

estudo

realizado

com

o

objetivo

de

verificar

a

aceitação

da

doação

de

oócitos,

ovorecepção

e

adoção

de

crianças

por

mulheres

inférteis

submetidas

a

tratamento

de

reprodução

assistida

demonstra

que

quase

metade

das

mulheres

não

doaria

seus

oócitos

por

não

querer

que

outra

mulher

carregue

sua

carga

genética

(Straehl

et

al,

2017).


Já

um

estudo

realizado

no

Irã

identificou

que,

apesar

do

crescimento

do

número

de

tratamentos

por

ovodoação

e

do

sucesso

terapêutico

observado

com

esses

procedimentos,

o

uso

de

oócitos

doados

pode

acarretar

desafios

aos

casais,

como

o

risco

de

transmissão

de

doenças

hereditárias,

além

de

questões

religiosas,

legais

e

culturais

(Ghelich-khani

et

al.

2020).

Em

contrapartida,

uma

revisão

sistemática

realizada

em

2016

mostrou

que

as

doadoras

que

compartilham

seus

óvulos

têm

o

desejo

de

auxiliar

outros

casais,

preocupando-se

com

bons

resultados

e

querendo

trazer

a

felicidade

para

o

outro

(Bracewell-Milnes

et

al,

2016).



O

número

de

casais

que

buscam

tratamentos

de

reprodução

humana

vem

crescendo

em

função

do

aumento

da

longevidade

e

dos

casamentos

tardios.

Outro

fator

que

faz

com

que

os

casais

busquem

por

tratamento

tardiamente

se

dá

em

função

da

inserção

da

mulher

no

mercado

de

trabalho

de

forma

efetiva

(Urata

et

al,

2024)

Sabe-se

que

a

idade

da

mulher

é

o

fator

prognóstico

mais

determinante

para

a

gestação.

Dessa

forma,

mulheres

após

os

40

anos

de

idade

normalmente

apresentam

uma

reserva

ovariana

diminuída

e

uma

qualidade

oocitária

menor

—

o

que

reduz

significativamente

a

chance

dessa

mulher

de

engravidar

e

aumenta

as

taxas

de

abortamento

nessa

faixa

etária.

Uma

alternativa

para

mulheres

que

possuem

uma

reserva

ovariana

muito

reduzida

ou

que,

até

mesmo,

já

se

encontram

no

período

da

menopausa

a

fertilização

in

vitro

óvulos

doados

de

teve

um

crescimento

nível

mundial,

que

possam

em

inférteis

em

função

da

idade/falência

ovariana

(Martinez

et

al,

2021).

Também

pode

ser

uma

opção

quando

há

anomalias

genéticas

possível

transmissão,

falha

em

FIVs

e

dificuldade

de

responder

ovariana

et

al,

2017).

Ghelich-Khani

tratamento

qualidade

com

especial

sua

saúde

mental.

Um

estudo

sobre

materna,

realizado

Sul

do

tratamentos

assistida

identificado

KEYWORDS

Quality

of

life;

egg

donation;

egg

reception;

infertility;

in

vitro

fertilisation.

Introduction

The

inability

to

conceive

causes

feelings

of

stress

for

most

women

who

experience

infertility.

According

to

the

World

Health

Organisation

(WHO),

one

in

six

people

will

be

affected

by

infertility

during

their

adult

lives,

representing

around

17.5%

of

the

population.

A

couple

is

considered

infertile

if,

after

12

months

of

trying

without

using

contraception,

they

are

unable

to

conceive

when

the

woman

is

up

to

35

years

old.


Reproductive

failure

has

significant

consequences

for

these

women,

especially

because,

in

many

cultures,

motherhood

still

represents

a

status

symbol

both

within

the

family

and

in

society.

Failure

to

achieve

this

goal

causes

couples

to

suffer

emotional

and

social

damage,

often

leading

to

isolationism

(Cosineau;

Domar,

2007).


The

difficulties

faced

in

this

context

of

infertility

can

often

interfere

with

the

quality

of

life

of

these

couples.

Quality

of

life

is

a

broad

concept

which,

according

to

the

WHO,

is

“an

individual’s

perception

of

their

position

in

life

in

the

context

of

the

culture

and

value

systems

in

which

they

live,

and

in

relation

to

their

goals,

expectations,

standards,

and

concerns”

(WHO,

1995),

encompassing

physical,

psychological,

social,

and

environmental

aspects.


The

obstacle

of

infertility

causes

many

couples

to

become

preoccupied

with

fertility

issues,

making

this

the

central

focus

of

their

married

life

and

neglecting

other

important

aspects

of

life

(Cosineau;

Domar,

2007).

According

to

Celda-Bélichon

et

al

(2025),

infertile

couples

experience

different

repercussions

on

their

quality

of

life.

While

men

are

more

affected

in

terms

of

their

relationship

with

their

partners,

women

suffer

greater

emotional,

physical,

and

social

damage.

Furthermore,

women

also

show

higher

rates

of

depressive

symptoms

during

the

treatment

period.


A

study

conducted

in

Spain

with

couples

from

Germany,

France,

and

Italy

assessed

the

quality

of

life

and

anxiety

levels

of

couples

who

travelled

to

the

country

to

undergo

IVF

with

donated

eggs.

The

findings

showed

that

results

differ

by

country

of

origin,

with

France

having

the

lowest

quality

of

life.

It

was

also

observed

that

women

have

a

lower

quality

of

life

and

greater

anxiety

than

men

(Madero

et

al.,

2017).

Due

to

technological

advances

in

assisted

reproduction,

such

as

in

vitro

fertilisation,

infertile

couples

now

have

greater

hope

in

their

desire

to

have

children

(Moutzouroulia

et

al,

2025).

In

addition,

oocyte

donation

has

become

a

new

treatment

modality

for

several

couples

seeking

to

have

a

child

(Montagnini,

2012).

However,

even

with

the

increase

in

this

type

of

treatment,

the

literature

remains

scarce

on

emotional

aspects

and

quality

of

life,

particularly

among

donors

and

recipients.

Oocyte

donation

is

regulated

by

the

Federal

Council

of

Medicine

(FCM)

in

Brazil

and

permits

shared

gamete

donation,

primarily

with

anonymity.

In

this

format,

the

donor

and

recipient

share

the

biological

material

and

the

financial

costs

of

assisted

reproduction

treatment.

It

is

important

to

emphasise

that

in

this

treatment

modality,

both

the

donor

(male

infertility)

and

the

recipient

(usually

a

decreased

ovarian

reserve)

present

some

limitations

to

spontaneous

conception

and

understand

that

treatment

through

donation

or

reception

is

the

best

way

to

achieve

pregnancy

(Oppenheimer

et

al.,

2018).

Generally,

recipients

have

already

come

a

long

way

from

the

diagnosis

of

infertility

to

the

recommendation

of

IVF

with

donated

eggs.

Throughout

this

process,

feelings

range

from

frustration

and

fear

to

anguish

and

hope.

When

women

accept

treatment

with

donated

eggs,

their

expectations

increase,

as

they

understand

that

donation

improves

their

chances

of

pregnancy

(Trindade

et

al.,

2025).

Therefore,

we

described

a

prospective

observational

study

that

included

donors,

recipients,

and

a

group

of

regular

IVF

patients

to

evaluate

the

impact

of

these

treatments

on

quality

of

life,

as

measured

by

FERTQOL.

Thus,

this

study

aims

to

understand

the

quality

of

life

of

women

undergoing

in

vitro

fertilisation

treatment,

with

an

emphasis

on

oocyte

donors

and

recipient

patients.

Materials

and

Methods

Study

population

This

prospective

cross-sectional

study

was

conducted

with

infertile

women

undergoing

assisted

reproduction

treatment.

Participants

were

recruited

from

an

assisted

reproduction

clinic

and

selected

according

to

inclusion

and

exclusion

criteria.

Women

undergoing

in

vitro

fertilisation

(IVF)

treatment

were

selected,

regardless

of

the

number

of

previous

treatments.

Sixty

women

with

infertility

participated

in

the

study

and

were

classified

into

the

following

groups:


Group

1:

15

oocyte

recipients;

Group

2:

19

egg

donors;

Group

3:

26

women

undergoing

treatment,

neither

donors

nor

recipients

(control

group).


The

data

were

collected

between

November

2023

and

March

2025.

Data

collection

began

after

approval

by

the

Ethics

and

Research

Committee,

under

number

AGHUse:

2022

-

0569

and

number

CAAE:

68406022.5.0000.5327.

In

addition,

all

participants

signed

a

free

and

informed

consent

form.

Procedures

The

patients

were

seen

by

the

psychologist

and,

during

the

appointment,

were

invited

to

participate

in

the

study.

This

consultation

usually

takes

place

before

the

start

of

treatment,

and

attendance

can

be

via

online

or

in-person.

If

accepted,

after

reading

and

signing

the

informed

consent

form,

the

sociodemographic

questionnaire

was

administered

together

with

the

FERTIQOL.

All

included

patients

from

groups

1

and

2

were

in

the

anonymous

modality.


Questionnaires

FERTIQOL

is

a

questionnaire

with

24

(twenty-four)

questions,

scored

from

0

(zero)

to

100

(one

hundred)

points,

which

assesses

the

quality

of

life

in

people

with

fertility

problems,

with

higher

scores

indicating

better

QoL.

The

results

are

divided

into

four

domains:

mind-body,

emotional,

relational,

and

social.

The

mind-body

domain

encompasses

physical

and

cognitive

health,

while

the

emotional

domain

addresses

the

impact

on

emotional

health.

The

relational

domain

encompasses

assessing

the

relationship

with

the

partner

and

social

issues

related

to

the

environment

(Boivin

et

al.,

2011b).

The

FERTIQOL

questionnaire

uses

a

5-point

Likert

scale

for

scoring,

with

scores

ranging

from

0

to

100;

higher

scores

indicate

better

quality

of

life.


The

sociodemographic

questionnaire

includes

variables

such

as

age,

education,

and

employment

status,

as

well

as

treatment

status

and

number

of

previous

pregnancies.


Sample

size

calculation

To

detect

a

15-point

difference

in

FertiQoL

scores,

assuming

a

score

of

75

in

the

control

group

and

60

in

the

study

group,

a

sample

size

of

16

women

per

group

was

required

(Pocock,

1983).

Statistical

analysis

The

collected

data

were

stored

in

Excel

and

subsequently

exported

to

the

JASP

program

for

analysis.

Three

main

statistical

models

were

used

to

perform

the

analyses:

One-way

ANOVA

(Analysis

of

Variance):

This

model

was

used

to

compare

whether

there

were

significant

differences

in

the

mean

total

FERTIQOL

score

among

the

three

treatment

groups

(TREATMENT

TYPE:

Recipients,

Donors,

and

IVF

with

own

oocytes).

Tukey’s

Post-hoc

Test:

After

the

ANOVA

confirmed

an

overall

difference,

this

test

was

applied

to

perform

pairwise

comparisons.

It

allowed,

for

example,

the

identification

that

the

IVF

with

its

own

oocyte

group

had

a

significantly

lower

quality

of

life

than

the

Donors

and

Recipients

groups,

while

the

latter

two

did

not

show

a

significant

difference

between

them.

Binary

Logistic

Regression:

This

model

was

used

to

calculate

Odds

Ratios

(OR).

For

this

purpose,

the

continuous

variable

“Quality

of

Life”

was

transformed

into

a

binary

variable

(0

=

Normal

Quality

of

Life;

1

=

Low

Quality

of

Life,

defined

by

cut-off

points

<

80

or

<

70).

The

regression

made

it

possible

to

estimate

the

risk

associated

with

variables

such

as:

Treatment

type

(especially

Type

3

–

IVF

with

own

oocytes),

psychotropic

medication,

months

of

attempts

and

age.

We

consider

the

level

of

significance

(p<5%)

statistically

relevant

for

our

data

comparison.

Discussion


Infertility

is

a

condition

that

affects

couples

both

physically

and

emotionally.

Understanding

this

phenomenon,

this

study

was

conducted

to

assess

the

quality

of

life

of

women

undergoing

treatment,

with

a

primary

focus

on

egg

donors

and

recipients.

As

we

demonstrated,

women

who

are

undergoing

treatment

without

donating

or

receiving

eggs

are

those

who

demonstrate

the

lowest

quality

of

life

in

the

emotional

sphere.

This

may

be

related

to

feelings

of

incapacity,

low

self-esteem,

and

high

levels

of

anxiety

and

depression

(Moutzouroulia

et

al,

2025),

which

are

perceived

from

the

diagnosis

of

infertility

and

throughout

treatment.


During

assisted

reproduction

treatment,

couples

experience

different

emotions,

and

this

can

lead

to

changes

in

their

relationship,

both

negative

and

positive.

Some

studies

indicate

difficulties

in

the

couple's

relationship

during

this

process,

especially

from

a

sexual

point

of

view,

where

they

mention

that

sexual

intercourse

becomes

mechanical

and

a

fulfilment

of

marital

duties.

Many

treatments

even

include

scheduled

sexual

intercourse,

which

turns

the

couple's

intimate

moments

into

an

obligatory

act,

potentially

leading

to

conflict

(Batista

et

al,

2016).


On

the

other

hand,

couples

also

show

greater

strengthening

of

their

relationship

and

improved

communication

when

their

peers

are

involved

in

treatment

(Batista

et

al.,

2016).

In

our

study,

the

results

corroborate

the

literature,

as

the

relational

domain

shows

high

scores

among

donors

and

recipients.

Furthermore,

among

the

domains

presented

in

FERTIQOL,

the

relational

average

has

the

highest

scores.


Couples

who

have

difficulty

conceiving

a

child

perceive

themselves

as

failures

from

a

social

standpoint,

leading

to

feelings

of

inferiority

in

relation

to

those

who

have

children.

In

addition,

they

also

feel

ashamed

and

tend

toward

social

isolation

(Peterson

et

al.,

2025).

Given

the

results

obtained

in

the

social

domain,

we

can

see

that

this

domain

was

the

one

that

had

the

greatest

negative

impact

on

the

quality

of

life

of

women

undergoing

assisted

reproduction

treatment,

with

the

lowest

scores

in

all

three

groups.

As

in

other

domains,

the

group

of

women

who

neither

donated

nor

received

eggs

also

had

a

lower

average

score

in

the

social

domain.

One

study

showed

that

people

who

share

their

infertility

with

others

have

fewer

depressive

symptoms

and

emphasise

how

important

social

support

is,

while

those

who

do

not

share

their

infertility

have

a

greater

sense

of

hopelessness

about

the

future

(Peterson

et

al,

2025).

Infertility

and

assisted

reproduction

treatment

have

significant

consequences

for

couples

experiencing

this

reality.

According

to

a

qualitative

study

conducted

in

the

Midwest

region

of

Brazil,

repeated

failed

attempts

to

conceive

diminish

the

couple's

well-being

and

quality

of

life.

The

authors

reveal

that

women

undergoing

treatment

show

feelings

of

guilt,

in

addition

to

experiencing

difficulties

in

social

relationships,

due

to

the

pressure

to

have

a

child

(Batista

et

al.,

2016).


Quality

of

life

is

a

broad

concept

that

aims

to

understand

the

well-being

of

each

individual.

QoL

is

influenced

by

physical,

emotional,

spiritual,

relational,

and

social

aspects

(Bueno-Sanchez

et

al,

2024).

The

total

FERTIQOL

score

represents

all

the

domains

already

presented,

such

as

mind/body,

emotional,

relational,

and

social.

Consistent

with

the

previous

results,

the

group

of

women

undergoing

treatment

without

donating

or

receiving

eggs

also

had

a

lower

total

FERTIQOL

score

than

the

group

of

donors

and

recipients.


In

addition

to

changes

in

quality

of

life,

women

with

infertility

experience

feelings

of

discrimination

and

judgment

from

others.

Receiving

a

diagnosis

of

infertility

is

often

associated

with

a

grieving

process,

due

to

the

loss

of

the

possibility

of

conceiving

a

child

naturally.

These

events

lead

to

feelings

of

worthlessness,

sadness,

and

increased

anxiety

in

these

women

(Vieira

&

Junior,

2023).

To

cope

with

the

complexity

of

treatment,

one

of

the

coping

strategies

used

by

couples

is

spirituality

and

religiosity

(Naab

et

al,

2025).

In

addition,

to

deal

with

fertility

issues

more

healthily,

it

is

also

important

to

seek

health

support

during

assisted

reproduction

treatment,

such

as

psychotherapy,

support

groups,

and

sometimes

psychiatric

support,

as

this

time

can

involve

negative

feelings,

resulting

in

high

levels

of

anxiety

and

depression

symptoms

(Yan

et

al.,

2024).

A

study

conducted

on

the

use

of

psychotropic

medication

among

women

seeking

assisted

reproduction

treatments

indicates

an

increased

risk

of

anxiety

disorders,

and

a

considerable

number

of

them

use

psychotropic

medicine

(Carvalho

et

al.,

2021).

In

the

present

study,

the

control

group

had

the

highest

rate

of

women

using

psychotropic

drugs

and

undergoing

psychotherapy.

In

addition,

we

observed

that

psychotherapy

is

still

the

strategy

most

commonly

used

by

women

undergoing

assisted

reproduction

treatment

to

cope

with

adverse

emotional

symptoms.

Another

important

point

to

mention

is

the

favourable

results

for

the

quality

of

life

of

donors

and

recipients.

A

study

conducted

with

this

group,

which

aimed

to

understand

these

women's

motivation,

concluded

that

their

behaviour

and

feelings

were

extremely

positive.

Also,

it

is

important

to

emphasise

that

donors'

main

motivation

is

to

help

other

women

altruistically

(Oppenheimer

et

al.,

2018).

Therefore,

for

recipients,

receiving

an

indication

for

treatment

with

donated

eggs

may

initially

cause

fear

and

surprise,

intensifying

the

impossibility

of

using

their

own

oocytes.

These

women

usually

experience

a

grieving

process

for

what

they

had

idealised.

With

acceptance,

a

feeling

of

hope

begins

to

prevail

in

these

women

(Montagnini

et

al.,

2023).

A

favourable

aspect

of

this

study

is

that

the

results

are

divided

into

donor,

recipient,

and

control

subgroups,

providing

a

better

understanding

of

the

specific

profiles

of

these

women

and

their

quality

of

life.

However,

the

main

limitation

of

this

study

is

that

it

examines

only

heterosexual

couples.

This

data

may

have

some

impact

because,

although

female

same-sex

couples

need

assisted

reproduction

procedures

to

achieve

pregnancy,

they

do

not

always

have

other

factors

contributing

to

infertility,

and

often

do

not

perceive

themselves

as

infertile.

Another

important

issue

is

that

we

do

not

include

patients

using

a

familiar

or

oocyte

bank

model

of

oocyte

donation.

These

patients

may

respond

differently

in

terms

of

quality

of

life

during

fertility

treatment.


In

conclusion,

patients

submitted

to

regular

IVF

(non-donors

or

oocyte

recipients)

are

at

extreme

risk

for

a

decreased

quality

of

life

and

consequently

an

increased

psychotropic

administration.

We

should

better

recognise

and

treat

these

patients

during

their

fertility

journey,

increasing

their

well-being

and

performing

a

more

comprehensive

and

patient-centred

reproductive

care.

ABSTRACT


Abstract

Introduction:

Having

of

this

affected

infertility,

affects

15%

of

worldwide.

high

prevalence,

assisted

reproduction

treatments

have

gained

notoriety

and

have

become

an

alternative

for

many

individuals.

Furthermore,

advances

in

medicine

have

significantly

increased

oocyte

donation,

which

can

have

a

profound

emotional

impact

on

both

egg

donors

and

recipients,

potentially

decreasing

the

of

life

(QoL)

of

these

women.

This

study

aims

to

assess

the

of

of

egg

donors

and

recipients,

as

well

as

infertile

women

who

will

undergo

assisted

reproduction

will

not

be

donors

or

recipients.

Prospective

cross-sectional

study

in

which

the

FERTIQOL

questionnaire

was

used

to

assess

QoL

and

a

sociodemographic

questionnaire

was

to

60

undergoing

treatment

at

an

assisted

reproduction

clinic

in

Porto

Alegre,

Rio

Grande

do

Sul.

According

to

the

collected

a

significant

difference

was

observed

in

the

total

FERTIQOL

score

(p<0.001).

In

the

covered

by

the

instrument,

the

results

were

also

significant,

with

mind

and

body

p<0.001,

emotional

p<0.001,

relational

p=0.040,

social

p=0.018.

26

total

and

all

domains,

compared

to

the

15

recipients

and

19

donors.

Conclusion:

Women

distress

who

KEYWORDS

Quality

of

life;

egg

donation;

egg

reception;

infertility;

in

vitro

fertilisation.

Introduction

The

inability

to

conceive

causes

feelings

of

stress

for

most

women

who

experience

infertility.

According

to

the

World

Health

Organisation

(WHO),

one

in

six

people

will

be

affected

by

infertility

during

their

adult

lives,

representing

around

17.5%

of

the

population.

A

couple

is

considered

infertile

if,

after

12

months

of

trying

without

using

contraception,

they

are

unable

to

conceive

when

the

woman

is

up

to

35

years

old.


Reproductive

failure

has

significant

consequences

for

these

women,

especially

because,

in

many

cultures,

motherhood

still

represents

a

status

symbol

both

within

the

family

and

in

society.

Failure

to

achieve

this

goal

causes

couples

to

suffer

emotional

and

social

damage,

often

leading

to

isolationism

(Cosineau;

Domar,

2007).


The

difficulties

faced

in

this

context

of

infertility

can

often

interfere

with

the

quality

of

life

of

these

couples.

Quality

of

life

is

a

broad

concept

which,

according

to

the

WHO,

is

“an

individual’s

perception

of

their

position

in

life

in

the

context

of

the

culture

and

value

systems

in

which

they

live,

and

in

relation

to

their

goals,

expectations,

standards,

and

concerns”

(WHO,

1995),

encompassing

physical,

psychological,

social,

and

environmental

aspects.


The

obstacle

of

infertility

causes

many

couples

to

become

preoccupied

with

fertility

issues,

making

this

the

central

focus

of

their

married

life

and

neglecting

other

important

aspects

of

life

(Cosineau;

Domar,

2007).

According

to

Celda-Bélichon

et

al

(2025),

infertile

couples

experience

different

repercussions

on

their

quality

of

life.

While

men

are

more

affected

in

terms

of

their

relationship

with

their

partners,

women

suffer

greater

emotional,

physical,

and

social

damage.

Furthermore,

women

also

show

higher

rates

of

depressive

symptoms

during

the

treatment

period.


A

study

conducted

in

Spain

with

couples

from

Germany,

France,

and

Italy

assessed

the

quality

of

life

and

anxiety

levels

of

couples

who

travelled

to

the

country

to

undergo

IVF

with

donated

eggs.

The

findings

showed

that

results

differ

by

country

of

origin,

with

France

having

the

lowest

quality

of

life.

It

was

also

observed

that

women

have

a

lower

quality

of

life

and

greater

anxiety

than

men

(Madero

et

al.,

2017).

Due

to

technological

advances

in

assisted

reproduction,

such

as

in

vitro

fertilisation,

infertile

couples

now

have

greater

hope

in

their

desire

to

have

children

(Moutzouroulia

et

al,

2025).

In

addition,

oocyte

donation

has

become

a

new

treatment

modality

for

several

couples

seeking

to

have

a

child

(Montagnini,

2012).

However,

even

with

the

increase

in

this

type

of

treatment,

the

literature

remains

scarce

on

emotional

aspects

and

quality

of

life,

particularly

among

donors

and

recipients.

Oocyte

donation

is

regulated

by

the

Federal

Council

of

Medicine

(FCM)

in

Brazil

and

permits

shared

gamete

donation,

primarily

with

anonymity.

In

this

format,

the

donor

and

recipient

share

the

biological

material

and

the

financial

costs

of

assisted

reproduction

treatment.

It

is

important

to

emphasise

that

in

this

treatment

modality,

both

the

donor

(male

infertility)

and

the

recipient

(usually

a

decreased

ovarian

reserve)

present

some

limitations

to

spontaneous

conception

and

understand

that

treatment

through

donation

or

reception

is

the

best

way

to

achieve

pregnancy

(Oppenheimer

et

al.,

2018).

Generally,

recipients

have

already

come

a

long

way

from

the

diagnosis

of

infertility

to

the

recommendation

of

IVF

with

donated

eggs.

Throughout

this

process,

feelings

range

from

frustration

and

fear

to

anguish

and

hope.

When

women

accept

treatment

with

donated

eggs,

their

expectations

increase,

as

they

understand

that

donation

improves

their

chances

of

pregnancy

(Trindade

et

al.,

2025).

Therefore,

we

described

a

prospective

observational

study

that

included

donors,

recipients,

and

a

group

of

regular

IVF

patients

to

evaluate

the

impact

of

these

treatments

on

quality

of

life,

as

measured

by

FERTQOL.

Thus,

this

study

aims

to

understand

the

quality

of

life

of

women

undergoing

in

vitro

fertilisation

treatment,

with

an

emphasis

on

oocyte

donors

and

recipient

patients.

have

about

the

future

and

assisted

reproduction

treatment

have

significant

consequences

for

couples

experiencing

this

reality.

According

to

a

qualitative

study

conducted

in

the

Midwest

region

of

repeated

failed

attempts

to

conceive

diminish

the

and

quality

of

authors

reveal

of

guilt,

to

experiencing

difficulties

in

social

relationships,

due

to

the

pressure

to

have

a

child

(Batista

et

al.,

2016).


Quality

of

life

is

a

broad

concept

that

aims

to

understand

the

well-being

of

each

individual.

QoL

is

influenced

by

physical,

emotional,

spiritual,

relational,

and

social

aspects

(Bueno-Sanchez

et

al,

2024).

The

total

FERTIQOL

score

represents

all

the

domains

already

presented,

such

as

mind/body,

emotional,

relational,

and

social.

Consistent

with

the

previous

results,

the

group

of

women

undergoing

treatment

without

donating

or

receiving

eggs

also

had

a

lower

total

FERTIQOL

score

than

the

group

of

donors

and

recipients.


In

addition

to

changes

in

quality

of

life,

women

with

infertility

experience

feelings

of

discrimination

and

judgment

from

others.

Receiving

a

diagnosis

of

infertility

is

often

associated

with

a

grieving

process,

due

to

the

loss

of

the

possibility

of

conceiving

a

child

naturally.

These

events

lead

to

feelings

of

worthlessness,

sadness,

and

increased

anxiety

in

these

women

(Vieira

&

Junior,

2023).

To

cope

with

the

complexity

of

treatment,

one

of

the

coping

strategies

used

by

couples

is

spirituality

and

religiosity

(Naab

et

al,

2025).

In

addition,

to

deal

with

fertility

issues

more

healthily,

it

is

also

important

to

seek

health

support

during

assisted

reproduction

treatment,

such

as

psychotherapy,

support

groups,

and

sometimes

psychiatric

support,

as

this

time

can

involve

negative

feelings,

in

high

levels

of

anxiety

and

depression

symptoms

et

al.,

2024).

A

study

conducted

on

the

use

of

psychotropic

medication

among

assisted

reproduction

an

increased

psychotropic

medicine

et

al.,

2021).

the

present

study,

the

control

group

had

the

highest

rate

of

women

using

psychotropic

drugs

and

undergoing

psychotherapy.

addition,

we

observed

that

psychotherapy

is

still

the

strategy

most

commonly

used

by

women

undergoing

assisted

reproduction

treatment

to

adverse

symptoms.

important

point

to

mention

is

the

favourable

results

for

the

of

life

of

donors

and

recipients.

A

study

conducted

with

this

group,

which

aimed

to

understand

these

women's

motivation,

concluded

that

their

behaviour

and

feelings

were

extremely

positive.

Also,

it

important

to

that

donors'

main

motivation

is

to

help

other

women

altruistically

(Oppenheimer

et

2018).

for

an

indication

for

treatment

with

eggs

cause

and

surprise,

intensifying

the

impossibility

of

using

their

oocytes.

usually

experience

a

grieving

for

what

they

had

idealised.

feeling

prevail

in

aspect

the
